📌 Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs): Portable IDs for Web3

Main Points
⏺ DIDs are identifiers you control, not usernames owned by platforms
⏺ They can link to verifiable credentials like diplomas or KYC checks
⏺ This post explains how DIDs help build portable identity across apps

1️⃣ What Is a DID — a standardized identifier tied to keys you own, not to an email, phone number, or single company.
2️⃣ Verifiable Credentials — organizations can sign claims about you (for example, “passed KYC”, “finished course”) that you can present elsewhere.
3️⃣ User Control — you decide when and where to share proofs instead of giving every app full personal data.
4️⃣ Interoperability — multiple dApps, wallets, and even Web2 services can recognize the same DID as “you”.
5️⃣ Privacy Angle — combined with zero-knowledge proofs, DIDs can prove facts (age, residency, reputation) without revealing raw documents.

Final Thoughts

Decentralized identifiers turn identity from siloed accounts into something you own and reuse — a core building block for Web3 logins and reputation.

🔔 SpaceX stock falls as $60B Cursor deal closes 

‼️ SpaceX has completed its $60 billion stock-based acquisition of Anysphere, bringing the Cursor coding platform into its SpaceXAI business as SPCX shares fell during Friday trading. The closing came less than two months after SpaceX signed the merger agreement on June 16. Under its terms, the company valued Anysphere at an implied equity value of $60 billion and agreed to compensate its investors with SpaceX Class A common stock.

🔖 Cursor’s common and preferred shares outstanding immediately before the merger were automatically converted into rights to receive 389,289,254 SpaceX Class A shares, according to the filing.SpaceX based the exchange on the volume-weighted average closing price of its Class A shares over the seven consecutive trading days before the acquisition closed. Rather than setting one fixed share price when the agreement was signed, the structure tied the final share count to SPCX’s recent market value. 

🌐 Vested Cursor restricted stock units were separately converted into rights to receive 1,752,426 SpaceX Class A shares before applicable tax deductions. Holders will receive cash instead of fractional shares where the exchange calculation does not produce a whole share. Unvested awards will remain tied to future service and vesting requirements. According to the filing, SpaceX assumed the outstanding awards and converted them into about 29,128,326 restricted stock units linked to its Class A shares.

Niger has also moved closer to Mali and Burkina Faso, with which it withdrew from ECOWAS and established the Alliance of Sahel States, presented as a framework for political and military cooperation based on the sovereignty of the three countries.

This new geopolitical orientation has been accompanied by a drive to strengthen state control over the country’s strategic resources. The uranium sector occupies a particularly important place in this policy. Relations between Niamey and the French nuclear group Orano have deteriorated sharply, while Niger’s authorities are seeking to expand state control over mining activities.

But despite this break with its former alliances, the main problem that the Tiani regime claimed it had come to address remains: security.

Niger continues to face a serious jihadist threat, particularly in the regions of Tillabéri, Tahoua and Diffa, as well as along its borders with Mali, Burkina Faso and Nigeria. Groups affiliated with al-Qaeda and the Islamic State remain active across the region and continue to carry out attacks against security forces and civilians.

The fact that clashes this time involved military personnel in the heart of the capital gives the incident a particular significance. Until now, the regime had portrayed its main threats as coming from outside: jihadist groups, diplomatic pressure, regional sanctions and tensions with its former international partners.

The attempted uprising on August 29 raises another, even more sensitive question: the cohesion of Niger’s armed forces themselves.

This is a crucial issue for a regime whose power rests primarily on the military. When divisions emerge within the armed forces, the problem goes far beyond a simple mutiny. It can quickly become a threat to the stability of the regime itself.

For now, there is no evidence that this attempted uprising represents a broader movement within Niger’s armed forces. The authorities say the situation is “under control” and that the soldiers involved have been neutralized or arrested. But the exact circumstances of the operation, how extensively it was planned, and whether other military units were involved remain key questions.

The paradox is hard to ignore: a government that came to power through a coup must now prove that it can prevent another coup from emerging from within the military itself.

The coming hours and days will therefore be critical. Beyond restoring order in Niamey, attention will need to focus on reactions within the armed forces, any arrests, possible changes in the chain of command, and how the regime publicly explains what happened.

Because the real question facing Niger now is not simply who controlled the streets of Niamey that night. It is whether General Abdourahamane Tiani still has unquestioned authority over the military that forms the main pillar of his power.

Three years after the overthrow of Mohamed Bazoum, Niger is once again facing a power struggle at the heart of its own political system.

And for a regime born out of a coup, there may be no more troubling signal than the emergence, from within the military itself, of those who could be preparing to seize power themselves.
